title: The way to the far shore
hook: sixteen young brahmins bring their questions, and each is answered

segments.voice: Yesterday: fish in shrinking water, and your line, fear born from the rod. Did you set down one stick? Today closes a week, and opens the last chapter of the Sutta Nipata. Day six hundred nine.

Far to the south, on the banks of the Godavari river, an old brahmin teacher named Bavari is living quietly when a visitor arrives, demands money, and, when Bavari has none to give, curses him: in seven days your head will split in seven pieces. Bavari is shaken. A kindly spirit tells him that the visitor knows nothing about heads splitting, but that there is someone in the north who does know: a Buddha. Bavari doesn't go himself. He sends his sixteen students instead. Today: the Parayana, the way to the far shore.
screen: `AN OLD TEACHER BY THE GODAVARI.` → `A CURSE, AND A FRIGHT.` → `SIXTEEN STUDENTS SENT NORTH.`

segments.voice: The prologue to the Sutta Nipata's fifth chapter traces their road north town by town, until they find the Buddha at a rocky shrine near Rajagaha. They ask Bavari's questions first, about the head and its splitting, and the Buddha answers that ignorance is the head, and knowledge, with faith, mindfulness and effort, is what splits it. Then each of the sixteen asks his own. Ajita asks what the world is wrapped in. Mettagu asks where suffering comes from. Upasiva asks what to lean on to cross. Hemaka, Todeyya, Kappa, Mogharaja: each brings something real, and each gets an answer shaped to him. That's the striking thing about this chapter. It isn't one teaching to a crowd. It's sixteen conversations. The word that names it, parayana, means the way to the beyond, the going to the far shore. And the image running through it is a flood: the rushing water of craving and views that has to be crossed. At the end, Pingiya, old and frail by his own account, goes home and sings the Buddha's praise to Bavari. Look back at the week: the dart of grief, only by deeds, the axe in the mouth, deep rivers are quiet, no view to cling to, fear from the rod. Six days in the Sutta Nipata. Now sixteen questions, and a river to cross.
screen: `A LONG ROAD NORTH.` · `IGNORANCE IS THE HEAD.` · `SIXTEEN QUESTIONS, SIXTEEN ANSWERS.` · `THE FLOOD TO BE CROSSED.` · then, large: `CROSSING THE FLOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your own question. Sit and settle. If you had walked that far to ask one question, what would it be? Not a clever one. The one that's actually there, under the others. Let it come slowly. When you have it, don't try to answer it. Just hold it, the way the students held theirs on the road. After the bell, if you like, write it down. The bell holds the time.
Parayana. The way to the far shore, the last chapter of the Sutta Nipata, where sixteen students each ask their question. Today's word.
Your line: crossing the flood. Today, carry your question with you, and notice where you look for an answer to it. Day six hundred nine.

howItsDone: The Parayanavagga is studied in Theravada monasteries and often taught one question at a time; its image of crossing the flood to the far shore runs through Buddhist chanting and teaching.

fork.setup: you're Bavari, old and frightened by a curse. a spirit tells you there is a Buddha far in the north. what do you do?
options: ignore it and wait out the seven days.
send your sixteen students, each with a question.
go after the man who cursed you.
fork.reveal: he stays, and sends his students. the questions they bring back fill the whole last chapter of the Sutta Nipata.

original.note: Pali parayana: the way to the beyond, the going to the far shore. the name of Sn 5.

trapdoor: what you thought: the far shore is somewhere you go after death.
what it means: in the Parayana it's the other side of the flood of craving and views, reached by the path.
what a scholar hears: the chapter's own closing lines explain its name: these teachings lead to the far shore, so this way of teaching is called Parayana.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 5 (Parayanavagga), prologue (vatthugatha) and sixteen questions

notes: Sn 5 paraphrased. Confirm the prologue details: Bavari on the Godavari, the visiting brahmin's curse (head split in seven), the deity's advice, the shrine near Rajagaha (Pasanaka cetiya).
Confirm the answer about the head: ignorance as the head, and knowledge with faith, mindfulness, concentration and energy as what splits it.
Confirm the sample questions attributed to Ajita (what the world is wrapped in) and Mettagu (where suffering comes from).
Confirm AN 3.32 quotes the Parayana by name (Udaya's question), or replace with another cross-reference.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the prologue doesn't say Bavari was too old to travel or that the students set out each with his own question, and gives no mileage; those were cut (hook, practice, myth, fork). 'The oldest of the sixteen, Pingiya' was a commentarial superlative; now 'old and frail by his own account' (Sn 5.18). The week look-back wrongly included day 602, which closed the previous week; it now covers 603 to 608. The trapdoor's 'thought by many to be very old' and the AN 3.32 cross-reference (which may quote Punnaka's question, not Udaya's) were replaced by the epilogue's own explanation of the name.
